builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Do "True" and "False" Add Up to One? Complement Consistency in LLM-Agent Opinion Simulations
summary: This is a validation procedure, not a component: it replaces the assumption that an agent's reported probability reflects a position on a claim by requiring the report on a claim and on its complement to sum to one, with an optional symmetrization step (averaging each answer with the complement of its paired answer) that doubles inference calls per state. Its cost is a parallel complementary-wording evaluation run and, if symmetrization is adopted in production, twice the sampling per reported probability, with no guarantee of improved accuracy since the symmetrized reports beat the better original wording at the final round for only one of three tested models. What can fail is precisely what the paper demonstrates in three small open models: paired reports exceed one on average, mirror populations diverge under feedback, and any downstream reading of simulated probabilities as beliefs can be invalid.
rationale: If the reader runs multi-agent opinion or survey simulations on small open models, this cheap wording-invariance check is a necessary precondition before trusting reported probabilities, so it should be piloted on their specific workload rather than adopted blindly as a fix.
technique: Complement-consistency testing for LLM-agent opinion reports
